items.title: Fossil fuel dispute threatens to derail COP31 climate deal
items.excerpt: Talks were set to resume at the UN COP31 summit on Sunday for a second day of overtime as countries struggle to reach a new global climate deal. Nations were deadlocked in Turkey on how to advance the fight against global warming, after new draft agreements included no reference to reducing the world's demand for fossil fuels. A third and "final" text was sent to delegates in the early hours of Sunday morning and members had until 06:00 local time (0300 GMT) to raise concerns before a 9am local time (0600GMT) meeting for approval. If countries cannot reach consensus - as required by the UN's climate talks process - the negotiations could be suspended to reconvene next year. A draft deal unveiled earlier this week called for a faster phase-out of fossil fuels, but a second, pared-down version released Thursday stripped away all mentions of coal, oil and gas - sparking threats of a walk out. The fallout led to the summit in Antalya blowing past the original deadline of Friday. On Saturday negotiating teams who had Sunday morning flights were rescheduling them - a sign a deal was still not in sight, and raising the risk that as teams eventually had to leave, the meeting could lose the critical numbers needed to pass an agreement. As part of a last ditch effort to produce an acceptable text, the European Union and Saudi Arabia - who were deeply divided over the future of fossil fuels - were brought together on Saturday to seek a compromise. ... COP31 President and Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum told delegates in the early hours of Sunday morning he believed concerns had been addressed. "We ask you to look at this decision carefully," Kurum said. "We are closer than ever to agreement on the remaining issues." If the countries can't agree, the summit would end with no deal and be reconvened next year.

items.title: US Consumers Are Holding Up Against Inflation Going Into Holiday Season
items.excerpt: Economists estimate inflation-adjusted personal spending rose by 0.1% in October from a month earlier, based on the Bloomberg survey's median estimate ahead of government figures due Wednesday. The modest increase builds on two robust quarters of consumer spending growth. The report, the highlight of a Thanksgiving holiday-shortened trading week, is also expected to show an acceleration in inflation. The personal consumption expenditures price index — the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation metric — is projected to rise 3.8% from October of last year. That's nearly double the Fed's goal and would match May as the biggest annual increase in three years. The core measure, which excludes the volatile food and energy categories, is also seen quickening, adding to evidence that Fed officials will raise interest rates at their December meeting. Steady job growth and solid economic activity this year from consumers and businesses alike are allowing US central bankers to focus squarely on mounting price pressures.

items.excerpt: Nov 20, 2026 ... Somewhere between 0.2% and 0.6% of inflation in core PCE over the past year is the product of high energy costs, according to a Dallas Fed report. ... Core personal consumption expenditures (PCE) is an inflation measure that is supposed to strip out the cost of food and energy because they’re so volatile — something the U.S. has been experiencing for a while now. But a new report from the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas shows that higher energy prices are showing up even in core PCE. It’s 3.1% higher than a year ago. Fed economists estimate that between 0.2% and 0.6% of that are the knock-on effects of high fuel prices. “Ultimately, energy costs have to work their way through the entire ecosystem,” said Rob Haworth, senior investment strategy director at U.S. Bank. “There's not much that shows up at our house or at our store without requiring a fossil fuel to get there.” Often, energy costs permeate the ecosystem through producer prices — the costs businesses charge each other. “If the transportation company or the the maker of the product — or ultimately the the retail store at the end — if they think they can raise prices and still sell as many units of of whatever, they will pass that cost along,” Haworth said.

items.title: Trump moves to limit congressional scrutiny before Democrats take power of Congress - The Times of India
items.excerpt: US president Donald Trump has ordered companies holding federal contracts to notify the White House before sharing information with Congress. He has also asked for them to withhold material the administration considers confidential, tightening his efforts to restrict congressional oversight ahead of Democrats taking control of Congress in January. The executive order, issued late Friday, applies to federal contractors and their subcontractors. Companies must coordinate with the White House and federal agencies on how to respond to congressional inquiries, including requests for information that the administration considers protected by executive privilege. The order warns that contractors failing to comply could have their existing contracts cancelled or be barred from future federal work. Democrats on their end are preparing to launch investigations into Trump's administration, family business dealings and the awarding of government contracts after winning control of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections. Federal contracts are expected to be a major focus of the inquiries, with Democrats raising concerns about government funds going to companies linked to Trump's family, particularly through the Pentagon. The order follows a directive issued earlier this week by White House counsel Will Scharf, who told federal agencies to seek approval from his office and the White House Office of Legislative Affairs before allowing employees to testify before Congress. Scharf has also argued that some Democratic investigations could amount to criminal conduct, a claim that has drawn criticism from lawmakers. Responding to the latest order, representative Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, called it a “blatant attack” on Congress' constitutional right to conduct oversight. He said Democrats would continue their investigations despite the administration's efforts to obstruct them. The White House defended the order as a measure to protect executive privilege and sensitive government communications, including those involving national security. It argued that contractors responding independently to congressional requests could disclose protected information and trigger costly legal disputes. Executive privilege allows presidents to shield certain confidential communications, particularly those involving White House deliberations. However, the protection is not absolute, and disputes over its scope can lead to prolonged legal battles. The order could face court challenges, particularly if contractors are directed to withhold information sought through congressional subpoenas. Democrats are preparing investigations into potential conflicts of interest, federal contracts, immigration enforcement and the administration's handling of the Jeffrey Epstein case.

items.title: Democrats won big in the midterms. Here's what they plan to do next | World News - Business Standard
items.excerpt: Democrats basking in their November 3 election wins will soon unveil an ambitious legislative agenda for the first 100 days and ​beyond, in a test of progressives' influence and Republicans' willingness to cooperate, as they take control of the US Congress on January 3. That agenda is likely to be unveiled in early December once a Senate leadership race is settled. It will mark a thunderous reversal of the past two years, when President Donald Trump's Republicans ruled the Senate and House of Representatives. With their narrow majorities, they rammed through major tax cuts skewed toward the rich and stood by as Trump grabbed their powers over tariffs and spending. Democrats' new majorities in Congress are anything but narrow. With a 56-44 majority in the Senate they are four votes short of the 60 votes needed to advance most legislation. In the House, their 257-172 force could grow beyond an 85-vote margin once a ‌handful of races are settled. ... "This is a realignment," said Democratic Senator Raphael Warnock of Georgia in a post-election ​interview with reporters. But in a warning to Democrats, veteran Republican Senator John Boozman of ​Arkansas said in an interview that despite his party's losses across the United States, Trump remains "a powerful force" and "I don't see any of his vetoes getting overridden" by Congress during his remaining two years in office. AGGRESSIVE AGENDA For ​months, Democrats have been plotting a House-Senate coordinated attack to undo Trump's major accomplishments, according to lawmakers and aides. With the high cost of living the top concern voiced by voters, Democratic leaders are going after the low-hanging fruit that also would help unite their party's progressives and moderates. Early votes are expected on legislation handcuffing Trump's ability to wage war on Iran without Congress' approval, which would help lower gasoline prices. Reversing Republicans' deep cuts to Medicaid and SNAP food stamp programs would begin helping the poor meet healthcare and grocery costs. Meanwhile, progressives have urged raising the federal minimum wage, which is unchanged since 2009 at $7.25 per hour. Some are pushing for $20 to $25. And in response to voter ​disgust over Washington ethics breaches, one of the first bills Democrats are expected to present is one barring lawmakers from insider trading of stocks. Republicans face a bind: joining Democrats could anger Trump unless he backs measures, while stonewalling could anger voters. "I think ‌there's a real understanding in Congress that things like healthcare, the really exorbitant premiums, you know, that people are having to pay" must be addressed, said Boozman, who was one of the Republicans ​who supported around $1 trillion in cuts to Medicare, Medicaid and Obamacare programs enacted last year.

items.title: FFM35: ‘Khadam’ sweeps 10 awards, Shaheizy Sam ends 15-year Best Actor drought as Malaysian cinema celebrates its finest | Malay Mail
items.excerpt: By Ian Jeremiah Patrick First Published: Sunday, 22 Nov 2026 10:13 AM MYT KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 22 — Horror ruled the night at the 35th Malaysia Film Festival (FFM35) yesterday as Khadam emerged as the biggest winner with 10 awards, while Shaheizy Sam made a triumphant return to Best Actor glory after 15 years. But the spotlight wasn’t entirely on the night’s biggest names. From promising newcomers to beloved industry veterans, the ceremony delivered its share of breakthrough wins, emotional speeches and career-defining moments. Held for the first time at Panggung Sari, Istana Budaya, the ceremony celebrated Malaysian cinema under the theme “Spectrum of Cinema”. Here are the biggest takeaways from FFM35. ‘Khadam’ makes a killing Horror film Khadam, directed by Shamyl Othman, dominated the ceremony with 10 awards from 12 nominations, including the coveted Best Film prize. The victory also earned the production a RM1 million incentive under the Creative Content Fund. ... — Picture courtesy of Finas Among its other wins were Best Director for Shamyl, Best Makeup for Jessie Yeow, Best Theme Song for Tak Berlagu, Best Sound Design for Soo Yuen Yiet and Best Original Score for Rendra Zawawi. The film also picked up Best Cinematography and Best Screenplay. Fourteen-year-old Ezarra Nurzhaffira won Best Supporting Actress for her portrayal of Puteh, while lead actress Aghniny Haque received a Special Jury Award. ... Shaheizy Sam’s 15-year comeback While Khadam swept the technical and major awards, Badak delivered another of the night’s biggest stories. Shaheizy Sam claimed Best Actor for his performance in the film, marking his first win in the category since Kongsi at FFM24 in 2011. The veteran actor reflected on the significance of the victory after years in the entertainment industry. “ Badak is a very meaningful work and a reminder to everyone. “I hope I can continue to humanise people through this industry,” he said. Aida Amron took home Best Actress for her portrayal of Mirah in ‘Badak’ at FFM35. ... His Badak co-star Aida Amron also celebrated a major victory, taking home Best Actress, while the film received a Special Jury Award. Meanwhile, a new generation of performers made its presence felt. Aila Azizul won Most Promising Actress for Astro Shaw’s Malam Terlarang, while Mierul Aiman, who recently played Kuda in Kudrat 1968, was named Most Promising Actor for Tarung: Unforgiven. ... items.title: Michael Jackson Biopic 'Michael' Skipping BAFTAs
items.excerpt: In a surprise move, the record-breaking box office smash Michael is skipping the BAFTAs, Deadline has confirmed. Antoine Fuqua’s billion-dollar film about the King of Pop won’t be submitted by producers GK Films or distributor Universal, which released internationally for Lionsgate. This takes the likes of Jaafar Jackson, Colman Domingo and the craft team out of the BAFTA equation. Variety first reported the news. Sources cited “multiple factors” behind the decision to us but declined to say what they are.
